screens.title: Administering Azure Cosmos DB
screens.narratorSegment: In this module you'll build a clear operational understanding of Azure Cosmos DB and how it differs from relational systems. We'll open with the core idea: Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL service designed for low-latency, high-scale workloads. You will learn how accounts, databases, and containers map to scalability and isolation, how partition keys determine data distribution, and how Request Units, or RUs, act as the performance currency for reads, writes, and queries. We'll walk through real administrative tasks: provisioning an account, creating a container with a partition key, inserting sample JSON documents, and running S Q L-like queries using the S Q L Core A P I. Along the way we'll clarify trade-offs — particularly how consistency models affect latency and availability — and highlight common mistakes, like choosing a poor partition key or missing indexing optimizations. By the end you should be able to provision a Cosmos account, pick sensible partition keys for predictable workloads, and monitor RU usage to prevent throttling. Keep an eye out for hands-on steps and a short query example you can reuse. What service-level decision would you make first when designing a global product: partitioning or consistency?

Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Administering Azure Cosmos DB

Administering Azure Cosmos DB

Global distribution, RUs, partitioning, and SQL API for JSON documents.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

This lesson gives a compact operational map: how accounts, databases, and containers relate to scalability and throughput; how to choose partition keys; and how RUs measure cost. You'll also see a short hands-on flow for provisioning and querying with the SQL (Core) API.

In this lesson
Core concepts, provisioning, RUs, partitioning, and indexing.
Coming up
Hands-on SQL API queries and sample JSON.
Practical goal
Provision a container that avoids hot partitions and monitors RU consumption.
Concept map
Accounts → Databases → Containers → Partitions → RUs
Account
Global distribution boundary. Holds databases and region replication settings.
Container
Unit of scalability and throughput. Define a partition key here.
Request Unit (RU)
Performance currency abstracting the cost of reads, writes, and queries per second.
Consistency
Choose from Strong to Eventual; each option trades latency and availability.
Key Takeaway

Cosmos DB is designed for global scale. Administrative decisions on partition keys, throughput, and consistency shape performance and cost.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus on operational skills you need as a Cosmos DB administrator. First, you'll be able to explain core concepts such as global distribution, multi-model APIs, and the set of consistency levels. This matters because those design choices determine latency, availability, and how applications behave across regions. Second, you'll provision and configure an Azure Cosmos DB account, database, and container. That includes choosing capacity mode, adding regions, and setting initial throughput so your environment supports production traffic. Third, you'll understand Request Units as the service's performance currency and learn strategies to provision, autoscale, and monitor RUs to avoid throttling. Fourth, you'll implement basic data operations using the S Q L Core A P I and tune indexing policies to reduce RU consumption when necessary. Each objective pairs a technical skill with a practical reason: global replication reduces read latency; correct partition keys prevent hot partitions; RU planning controls cost and responsiveness. These skills let you meet SLAs, optimize cost, and operate globally distributed NoSQL data stores reliably. Which objective will you practice first: provisioning, partitioning, or RU tuning?

screens.title: Skills Breakdown
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide breaks the skills down into practical tasks and the mental models you will use. You will map accounts to global replication and databases to logical isolation, and you will treat containers as the unit of throughput and partitioning. For partition keys, the mental model is distribution: choose a property that spreads writes and reads evenly so no single partition becomes a bottleneck. For RUs, think of a rate limit budget that operations consume; monitoring query RU charges lets you tune indexing and throughput to match workload patterns. For indexing, the model is selectivity: automatic indexing is flexible but can increase RU cost; pruning indexes or adding composite indexes for common query shapes reduces cost. Finally, we'll practice a hands-on flow: create an account, a database and container with a partition key, insert sample JSON documents, and run queries while watching RU charge. These practical steps connect the mental models to the Azure portal actions you'll perform and clarify why each configuration choice matters for scale, latency, and cost.

screens.title: What is Cosmos DB?
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database service built for predictable low latency and elastic scale. As a definition, treat it as a managed service that stores data in non-tabular forms—commonly JSON documents, key-value pairs, or graph structures—and exposes different APIs so applications can use familiar protocols. The multi-model aspect means you can interact with the same service through the S Q L (Core) A P I for JSON documents, MongoDB-compatible APIs, Cassandra, Gremlin for graph data, or the Table A P I for key-value patterns. Practically, that versatility makes Cosmos DB useful when a system needs flexible schemas, massive horizontal scale, and regionally close reads for global users. An example: an international product catalog with user reviews benefits from JSON document storage and global distribution to serve readers in multiple continents with minimal latency. A common misconception is to treat Cosmos DB like a relational replacement; while it can store structured data, it lacks relational ACID semantics across containers and instead offers different consistency choices. Key takeaway: use Cosmos DB when you need global scale, flexible models, and predictable latency, and choose the A P I that best matches your application's data access pattern.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Cosmos DB is a managed, globally distributed NoSQL service that supports multiple data models via different APIs, ideal for low-latency, flexible-schema scenarios.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › What is Cosmos DB?
Definition

Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft's managed, globally distributed NoSQL database service supporting multiple models and APIs for flexible application needs.

Multi-model: documents, key-value, graph; choose an API that matches your app.

Globally distributed: replicate data to regions for low-latency reads and disaster recovery.

Throughput model: operations consume Request Units that you provision or autoscale.

Example
An international product catalog stored as JSON, replicated to several regions for low-latency product reads.
Misconception
Cosmos DB is not a drop-in relational replacement; its trade-offs involve consistency models and partitioning, not relational joins between containers.
Multi-model APIs
SQL (Core)
JSON document queries using a SQL-like language.
MongoDB API
MongoDB wire protocol compatibility for document apps.
Gremlin
Graph data model for connected data and traversals.
Key Takeaway

Pick the API that maps to your data model. Use Cosmos DB when you need flexible schemas, global replication, and predictable low latency.

screens.title: Accounts, Databases, and Containers
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the resource hierarchy is fundamental to administration. In Cosmos DB, the account is the top-level boundary you create in Azure; it controls global distribution settings and acts as the management boundary for databases and containers. Within the account, databases provide logical grouping; they are convenient for organizing sets of containers and for applying throughput at the database level when desired. Containers, sometimes called collections or tables depending on A P I, are the primary unit of scalability and throughput. When you create a container you choose a partition key and set throughput either at the container or database level. The partition key determines how items are distributed to physical partitions, which in turn affects parallelism and storage layout. A concrete example: creating a products container for an e-commerce system and selecting /category as a partition key will group products by category across partitions. A common administration mistake is to place unrelated datasets into a single container to save accounts; that sacrifices isolation and complicates throughput management. Key takeaway: design your resource hierarchy to match isolation, scale, and throughput needs. How will you partition datasets to balance these concerns?

keyIdea.title: Resource hierarchy
keyIdea.text: Account → Database → Container. Containers are the unit of scale and throughput; choose partitioning and throughput placement deliberately.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Accounts, Databases, and Containers
Resource boxes
Account
Global distribution boundary and management scope for regions and keys.
Database
Logical grouping of containers; optional throughput at database level.
Container
Unit of scalability and throughput. Define partition key here.
Administration tip

Place datasets that share throughput and partitioning patterns in the same container. Keep unrelated workloads in separate containers to simplify scaling and RBAC.

Partitioning callout
When creating a container you select a partition key path such as /category. That key determines distribution across physical partitions and therefore the container's ability to scale horizontally.
Example
Products container with partition key /category groups similar items and attempts to distribute load by category.
Common mistake
Using a narrowly distributed key that causes a hot partition under heavy write or read traffic.
Key Takeaway

Match resource hierarchy to isolation and scale needs. Containers are your scaling units; partition keys decide distribution.

screens.title: Provisioning a Cosmos DB Account and Container
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning a Cosmos DB account and a container is an essential administrative task. The process starts in the Azure portal where you create a new Azure Cosmos DB account and select the A P I—Core (S Q L) for JSON documents in our hands-on example. Next, pick subscription and resource group, then provide a globally unique account name and select an initial region or regions for replication. Choose capacity mode—provisioned throughput or autoscale—and decide whether to apply throughput at the database or container level. Once the account is deployed, open Data Explorer and create a database and container. When creating the container choose a container ID and a partition key path like /category or /userId. If you choose 400 RUs for a container, Cosmos DB guarantees that throughput for that container. After creation you can insert sample JSON documents and run S Q L queries to verify data and inspect RU charges. A frequent operational decision is whether to enable autoscale; autoscale simplifies operations by expanding RUs within a range but impacts cost. Remember to monitor RU usage after provisioning to tune throughput and avoid throttling. What monitoring signals will tell you to increase throughput or adjust partitioning?

Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Provisioning a Cosmos DB Account
Provisioning steps
1
Create account and select API
Choose Core (SQL) for JSON documents or another API that matches your application.
2
Select regions and capacity mode
Pick regions for low-latency reads and choose between provisioned and autoscale throughput.
3
Create database and container
Provide database ID, container ID, select partition key, and set throughput at container or database level.
Verification
Insert sample JSON documents and run sample queries. Observe the Query Stats to see RU charge for each query and adjust throughput or indexing as needed.
Example
Create a products database and container, choose /category as partition key, and set 400 RUs to start.
Watch
Monitor RU consumption and throttling. If queries are expensive, inspect indexing or increase RUs rather than over-provisioning blindly.

screens.title: Partition Keys and Hot Partitions
screens.narratorSegment: Partition keys determine how Cosmos DB distributes data across physical partitions, and they directly impact performance and scalability. Define a partition key as a property path in your JSON documents, for example /category or /userId. The goal is even distribution: a good partition key produces many logical partitions that map across physical partitions so reads and writes can be served in parallel. A classic example is an e-commerce catalogue: using /category can spread products, but if one category receives most of the traffic you can still create hot partitions. A hot partition occurs when a single logical partition receives a disproportionate amount of requests; the result is throttling regardless of total provisioned RUs. Common fixes include choosing a more granular key, designing a synthetic key by combining properties, or reshaping traffic to spread requests. A frequent misconception is to choose keys based only on uniqueness; uniqueness alone doesn't guarantee even traffic distribution. Key takeaway: select partition keys by expected access patterns and monitor for hot partitions in production. Ask yourself: which property will spread write and read load most evenly for my workload?

keyIdea.text: Choose a partition key that evenly distributes workload. Avoid keys that concentrate reads or writes, and monitor for hot partitions.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Partition Keys and Hot Partitions
Partition key definition

A partition key is a JSON property path used to distribute items across logical and physical partitions. It controls parallelism and storage layout.

Good partition keys: spread writes and reads, remain present on most documents, and avoid skew.
Poor keys: single-value fields, very small cardinality, or keys that map high percentage of traffic to one partition.
Scenario
If /userId distributes evenly across users, it may be better than /region which could concentrate traffic.
Hot partition
A busy category that receives most writes will create a hot partition and can cause throttling even with adequate RUs overall.
Design patterns
Synthetic keys
Combine fields, for example category:region, to increase cardinality and reduce hotspots.
Re-evaluate with metric data
Monitor partition RU consumption and request distribution to validate your choice and adjust if needed.
Key Takeaway

Partition keys should be chosen for expected access patterns, not only uniqueness. Monitor and adapt if you see hotspots.

screens.title: Request Units (RUs): The Performance Currency
screens.narratorSegment: Request Units, or RUs, are the abstract measure Cosmos DB uses to represent the system resources consumed by operations. Think of RUs as a normalized budget: reads, writes, queries, and stored procedure executions each consume a certain RU amount. When you provision 400 RUs for a container, Cosmos DB guarantees capacity for operations totaling 400 RUs per second on that container. Queries that scan many documents or execute complex predicates consume more RUs than targeted point reads. For example, a cross-partition query that must examine many partitions will often have a higher RU charge. Monitoring RU consumption is central to administration: the portal's Query Stats shows RU charge per query, and the metrics view shows RU consumption over time. If you exceed your provisioned RUs, requests are throttled and receive 429 responses until capacity frees up. To avoid throttling, either increase provisioned RUs, enable autoscale to expand RUs automatically, or optimize queries and indexing to reduce RU costs. A common misconception is that adding more RUs fixes poor partitioning; while RUs help with throughput, partitioning and index optimization are necessary to prevent inefficient cross-partition operations. The closing question: what pattern of RU consumption would alert you to a cross-partition scan?

keyIdea.text: RUs measure resource cost of database operations. Monitor RU charge and tune throughput, indexing, or partitioning to prevent throttling.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Request Units (RUs)
What is an RU?

An RU is a performance currency that abstracts compute, I/O, and memory cost for a database operation. Operations consume RUs; you provision capacity in RUs per second.

Point reads are cheap; full scans and cross-partition queries are expensive.
Provision at container or database level. Autoscale can expand RUs automatically within a range.
Monitor
Use Query Stats to see RU cost per query and metrics to view RU consumption trends. Throttling (429) means RU limits were exceeded.
Practical tips
Reduce RU cost
Optimize queries and indexing. Avoid cross-partition scans by using filters on the partition key when possible.
Autoscale
Autoscale adjusts RUs automatically within a range, simplifying management for variable workloads.
Key Takeaway

Track RU charge per operation and tune queries, indexes, and throughput to meet SLAs without waste.

screens.title: Autoscale vs Provisioned Throughput
screens.narratorSegment: Throughput management in Cosmos DB comes in two modes: provisioned throughput and autoscale. Provisioned throughput sets a fixed RU per second for a container or database, which you manage manually. Autoscale removes the need to set a single fixed number by allowing Cosmos DB to scale RUs automatically within a configured range, increasing capacity during peaks and dropping when demand falls. This simplifies operations for variable workloads, but you should understand the cost implications and the scaling limits you configure. Operationally, autoscale is useful when workloads are spiky or unpredictable; provisioned throughput is appropriate for steady, predictable workloads where you can plan costs. In either case, you must monitor RU consumption and throttling signals. An incorrect assumption is to rely on autoscale to hide design problems: autoscale helps with temporary spikes but does not fix inefficient queries or bad partitioning. A concrete example: if nightly batch jobs spike reads across all partitions, autoscale can accommodate the increased RU demand without manual intervention. Key takeaway: choose autoscale for variable traffic and provisioned throughput for cost predictability, but always optimize queries and partitioning first.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Autoscale vs Provisioned
Throughput choices
Autoscale · Provisioned
Autoscale
Automatically scales RUs within a configured range as demand changes. Good for spiky workloads and reduces manual changes.
Provisioned
Fixed RU capacity per second. Predictable costs for stable workloads and simpler budgeting.
Example
Nightly spikes from batch processing can be handled by autoscale, while a high-traffic public API with stable demand might use provisioned throughput for cost predictability.
Misconception
Autoscale does not replace good design. It covers capacity but does not fix inefficient queries or poor partition keys that cause hotspots.
Key Takeaway

Choose autoscale for variable, spiky traffic. For steady workloads, use provisioned throughput. Always optimize queries and partitioning first.

screens.title: Using the SQL (Core) API to Query JSON Documents
screens.narratorSegment: The S Q L (Core) A P I lets you query JSON documents with a S Q L-like language. You will run queries to select specific fields, filter by properties, and order results. A practical example from the chapter selects product id, name, and price where category equals Electronics and prices are above a threshold. The key operational detail is to watch the Query Stats for RU charge — queries that filter by partition key are cheaper because they target a single partition. In contrast, queries that don't include the partition key often become cross-partition scans and cost more RUs. Let's walk through a short query example that you can paste into Data Explorer. Use point reads when possible for single-item fetches; for collection queries, ensure you have helpful indexes. After you run queries, inspect Query Stats and note the RU charge; if it's high, consider adding a composite index or including the partition key in the filter. Closing question: when you see a high RU charge for a query, which three actions will you consider first: add an index, include partition filter, or increase RUs?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › SQL (Core) API Queries
Query example
Run the following SQL-like query in Data Explorer to inspect product documents and RU charge.
-- Example: Query documents in a Cosmos DB container (SQL API)
SELECT c.id, c.productName, c.price
FROM c
WHERE c.category = 'Electronics' AND c.price > 100
ORDER BY c.price DESC
Tip: Include the partition key in the WHERE clause when possible to avoid cross-partition queries and to lower RU charges. After running the query, review Query Stats to see RU charge, and then iterate.
Example scenario
Query products where category equals Electronics and price over 100 to return id, name and price ordered by price.
Query Stats

Observe RU charge per query in Data Explorer. High values indicate cross-partition scans or non-indexed predicates.

Key Takeaway

Prefer point reads and partition-key filtered queries to minimize RU cost. Use composite indexes for frequent multi-attribute queries.

screens.title: Indexing Policies and RU Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Cosmos DB indexes all properties by default, which provides flexibility for ad-hoc queries but can increase RU consumption for large datasets or specific query patterns. Indexing policy customization is an important administrative tool: you can exclude paths you never query, add included paths for frequently queried properties, and define composite indexes that optimize multi-property ORDER BY or WHERE clauses. For example, if you frequently query by category and then sort by price, a composite index on (category, price) will reduce RU charges for those queries. The trade-off is that more indexes increase write RU cost because each write must update indexes. A common administration pattern is to start with automatic indexing during development for agility, then refine indexing policies before production by excluding rarely-used paths and adding composites for hot query shapes. Monitor RU impact by comparing RU charge before and after policy changes. A misconception is to remove too many indexes to save write RU at the expense of expensive read queries — balance is key. Final question: when you observe high RU reads on a frequent query, which indexing change would you try first?

Indexing modes

Automatic indexing includes all paths by default. Refine indexing to include composite paths or exclude rarely-used paths to lower RU cost for writes or reads as needed.

Composite index example: for queries filtering by category and ordering by price, add (category, price) to the composite index list.
Exclude index paths for large, seldom-searched properties to reduce write RU costs.
Practical checklist
  • Start with automatic indexing during development for flexibility.
  • Before production, identify hot queries and add composite indexes for them.
  • Exclude large irrelevant paths to reduce write RU costs.
Key Takeaway

Optimize indexing based on actual query patterns: composites for multi-field queries and exclusions for rarely queried paths.

screens.title: Consistency Levels: Trade-offs Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Cosmos DB provides five well-defined consistency levels: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual. Each level is a trade-off between consistency guarantees and latency/availability. Strong consistency gives the most synchronous guarantee: reads always reflect the latest committed write, but it increases cross-region latency and reduces availability in certain failure scenarios. Bounded Staleness guarantees reads lag by no more than a specified version or time window. Session consistency is a practical default for many applications because it guarantees monotonic reads and read-your-own-writes within a session while allowing better latency across regions. Consistent Prefix guarantees that reads never see out-of-order writes, and Eventual provides the weakest guarantees but the lowest latency and highest availability. A real-world example: a shopping cart that must show a user's own latest changes benefits from Session consistency, while a global analytics feed that can tolerate slight delays might use Eventual. A common misconception is that Strong is always the safest choice; in global deployments Strong can introduce unacceptable latency. Key takeaway: choose the weakest consistency that still meets your correctness requirements to reduce latency and improve availability.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.5 › Consistency Levels
Consistency comparison
Strong
Latest reads guaranteed; higher latency.
Bounded Staleness
Reads lag by a configured amount.
Session
Good balance: read-your-writes in a session.
Consistent Prefix
No out-of-order writes; eventual completeness.
Eventual
Lowest latency and highest availability; eventual convergence.
Example
Shopping cart user experience: Session consistency ensures users see their own recent writes without forcing global Strong consistency.
Misconception
Strong consistency is not always best for global apps because of cross-region latency penalties.
Key Takeaway

Choose the weakest consistency that satisfies correctness to reduce latency and improve availability. Session is often a pragmatic default.

screens.title: Common Administration Tasks and Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Administrative tasks for Cosmos DB include monitoring RU consumption, adjusting throughput, managing global distribution, configuring backups, and implementing security controls like RBAC and network restrictions. Monitoring RU trends and query RU charge helps you decide whether to scale RUs, refine indexes, or change partitioning strategies. Backup and restore configuration is important for recovery; ensure you understand the account-level backup cadence and retention options as part of operational planning. Security requires role-based access control to restrict management operations and network controls such as service endpoints or Private Link to limit network exposure. When troubleshooting performance, common culprits include hot partitions, inefficient queries causing high RU charge, and missing composite indexes for frequent multi-attribute queries. A frequent mistake is reacting only by increasing RUs without investigating whether a partition key or index change would reduce RU consumption more effectively. Another is assuming a single account should hold all datasets when isolation and throughput management would be simpler with multiple accounts or containers. Key takeaway: pair monitoring with targeted optimizations — scaling alone is only part of the solution. What is the first telemetry you will check when a workload shows spikes?

Operational checklist
Monitor
Track RU consumption, throttling (429s), and per-partition metrics to detect hotspots early.
Backups
Understand account-level backup settings and restore procedures as part of your recovery plan.
Security
Use RBAC, keys and network controls such as VNet service endpoints or Private Link to limit access.
Troubleshooting
When you see throttling, inspect per-partition RU usage, query RU charges, and indexing policies before increasing RUs.
Common mistake
Scaling RUs without addressing hot partitions or inefficient queries often wastes cost and fails to solve latency issues.
Key Takeaway

Pair telemetry with targeted fixes: investigate hotspots and query costs before increasing throughput. Secure and back up your account as part of operations.

fullNarratorScript:
In this module you'll build a clear operational understanding of Azure Cosmos DB and how it differs from relational systems. We'll open with the core idea: Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL service designed for low-latency, high-scale workloads. You will learn how accounts, databases, and containers map to scalability and isolation, how partition keys determine data distribution, and how Request Units, or RUs, act as the performance currency for reads, writes, and queries. We'll walk through real administrative tasks: provisioning an account, creating a container with a partition key, inserting sample JSON documents, and running S Q L-like queries using the S Q L Core A P I. Along the way we'll clarify trade-offs — particularly how consistency models affect latency and availability — and highlight common mistakes, like choosing a poor partition key or missing indexing optimizations. By the end you should be able to provision a Cosmos account, pick sensible partition keys for predictable workloads, and monitor RU usage to prevent throttling. Keep an eye out for hands-on steps and a short query example you can reuse. What service-level decision would you make first when designing a global product: partitioning or consistency?

These learning objectives focus on operational skills you need as a Cosmos DB administrator. First, you'll be able to explain core concepts such as global distribution, multi-model APIs, and the set of consistency levels. This matters because those design choices determine latency, availability, and how applications behave across regions. Second, you'll provision and configure an Azure Cosmos DB account, database, and container. That includes choosing capacity mode, adding regions, and setting initial throughput so your environment supports production traffic. Third, you'll understand Request Units as the service's performance currency and learn strategies to provision, autoscale, and monitor RUs to avoid throttling. Fourth, you'll implement basic data operations using the S Q L Core A P I and tune indexing policies to reduce RU consumption when necessary. Each objective pairs a technical skill with a practical reason: global replication reduces read latency; correct partition keys prevent hot partitions; RU planning controls cost and responsiveness. These skills let you meet SLAs, optimize cost, and operate globally distributed NoSQL data stores reliably. Which objective will you practice first: provisioning, partitioning, or RU tuning?

This second objectives slide breaks the skills down into practical tasks and the mental models you will use. You will map accounts to global replication and databases to logical isolation, and you will treat containers as the unit of throughput and partitioning. For partition keys, the mental model is distribution: choose a property that spreads writes and reads evenly so no single partition becomes a bottleneck. For RUs, think of a rate limit budget that operations consume; monitoring query RU charges lets you tune indexing and throughput to match workload patterns. For indexing, the model is selectivity: automatic indexing is flexible but can increase RU cost; pruning indexes or adding composite indexes for common query shapes reduces cost. Finally, we'll practice a hands-on flow: create an account, a database and container with a partition key, insert sample JSON documents, and run queries while watching RU charge. These practical steps connect the mental models to the Azure portal actions you'll perform and clarify why each configuration choice matters for scale, latency, and cost.

Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database service built for predictable low latency and elastic scale. As a definition, treat it as a managed service that stores data in non-tabular forms—commonly JSON documents, key-value pairs, or graph structures—and exposes different APIs so applications can use familiar protocols. The multi-model aspect means you can interact with the same service through the S Q L (Core) A P I for JSON documents, MongoDB-compatible APIs, Cassandra, Gremlin for graph data, or the Table A P I for key-value patterns. Practically, that versatility makes Cosmos DB useful when a system needs flexible schemas, massive horizontal scale, and regionally close reads for global users. An example: an international product catalog with user reviews benefits from JSON document storage and global distribution to serve readers in multiple continents with minimal latency. A common misconception is to treat Cosmos DB like a relational replacement; while it can store structured data, it lacks relational ACID semantics across containers and instead offers different consistency choices. Key takeaway: use Cosmos DB when you need global scale, flexible models, and predictable latency, and choose the A P I that best matches your application's data access pattern.

Understanding the resource hierarchy is fundamental to administration. In Cosmos DB, the account is the top-level boundary you create in Azure; it controls global distribution settings and acts as the management boundary for databases and containers. Within the account, databases provide logical grouping; they are convenient for organizing sets of containers and for applying throughput at the database level when desired. Containers, sometimes called collections or tables depending on A P I, are the primary unit of scalability and throughput. When you create a container you choose a partition key and set throughput either at the container or database level. The partition key determines how items are distributed to physical partitions, which in turn affects parallelism and storage layout. A concrete example: creating a products container for an e-commerce system and selecting /category as a partition key will group products by category across partitions. A common administration mistake is to place unrelated datasets into a single container to save accounts; that sacrifices isolation and complicates throughput management. Key takeaway: design your resource hierarchy to match isolation, scale, and throughput needs. How will you partition datasets to balance these concerns?

Provisioning a Cosmos DB account and a container is an essential administrative task. The process starts in the Azure portal where you create a new Azure Cosmos DB account and select the A P I—Core (S Q L) for JSON documents in our hands-on example. Next, pick subscription and resource group, then provide a globally unique account name and select an initial region or regions for replication. Choose capacity mode—provisioned throughput or autoscale—and decide whether to apply throughput at the database or container level. Once the account is deployed, open Data Explorer and create a database and container. When creating the container choose a container ID and a partition key path like /category or /userId. If you choose 400 RUs for a container, Cosmos DB guarantees that throughput for that container. After creation you can insert sample JSON documents and run S Q L queries to verify data and inspect RU charges. A frequent operational decision is whether to enable autoscale; autoscale simplifies operations by expanding RUs within a range but impacts cost. Remember to monitor RU usage after provisioning to tune throughput and avoid throttling. What monitoring signals will tell you to increase throughput or adjust partitioning?

Partition keys determine how Cosmos DB distributes data across physical partitions, and they directly impact performance and scalability. Define a partition key as a property path in your JSON documents, for example /category or /userId. The goal is even distribution: a good partition key produces many logical partitions that map across physical partitions so reads and writes can be served in parallel. A classic example is an e-commerce catalogue: using /category can spread products, but if one category receives most of the traffic you can still create hot partitions. A hot partition occurs when a single logical partition receives a disproportionate amount of requests; the result is throttling regardless of total provisioned RUs. Common fixes include choosing a more granular key, designing a synthetic key by combining properties, or reshaping traffic to spread requests. A frequent misconception is to choose keys based only on uniqueness; uniqueness alone doesn't guarantee even traffic distribution. Key takeaway: select partition keys by expected access patterns and monitor for hot partitions in production. Ask yourself: which property will spread write and read load most evenly for my workload?

Request Units, or RUs, are the abstract measure Cosmos DB uses to represent the system resources consumed by operations. Think of RUs as a normalized budget: reads, writes, queries, and stored procedure executions each consume a certain RU amount. When you provision 400 RUs for a container, Cosmos DB guarantees capacity for operations totaling 400 RUs per second on that container. Queries that scan many documents or execute complex predicates consume more RUs than targeted point reads. For example, a cross-partition query that must examine many partitions will often have a higher RU charge. Monitoring RU consumption is central to administration: the portal's Query Stats shows RU charge per query, and the metrics view shows RU consumption over time. If you exceed your provisioned RUs, requests are throttled and receive 429 responses until capacity frees up. To avoid throttling, either increase provisioned RUs, enable autoscale to expand RUs automatically, or optimize queries and indexing to reduce RU costs. A common misconception is that adding more RUs fixes poor partitioning; while RUs help with throughput, partitioning and index optimization are necessary to prevent inefficient cross-partition operations. The closing question: what pattern of RU consumption would alert you to a cross-partition scan?

Throughput management in Cosmos DB comes in two modes: provisioned throughput and autoscale. Provisioned throughput sets a fixed RU per second for a container or database, which you manage manually. Autoscale removes the need to set a single fixed number by allowing Cosmos DB to scale RUs automatically within a configured range, increasing capacity during peaks and dropping when demand falls. This simplifies operations for variable workloads, but you should understand the cost implications and the scaling limits you configure. Operationally, autoscale is useful when workloads are spiky or unpredictable; provisioned throughput is appropriate for steady, predictable workloads where you can plan costs. In either case, you must monitor RU consumption and throttling signals. An incorrect assumption is to rely on autoscale to hide design problems: autoscale helps with temporary spikes but does not fix inefficient queries or bad partitioning. A concrete example: if nightly batch jobs spike reads across all partitions, autoscale can accommodate the increased RU demand without manual intervention. Key takeaway: choose autoscale for variable traffic and provisioned throughput for cost predictability, but always optimize queries and partitioning first.

The S Q L (Core) A P I lets you query JSON documents with a S Q L-like language. You will run queries to select specific fields, filter by properties, and order results. A practical example from the chapter selects product id, name, and price where category equals Electronics and prices are above a threshold. The key operational detail is to watch the Query Stats for RU charge — queries that filter by partition key are cheaper because they target a single partition. In contrast, queries that don't include the partition key often become cross-partition scans and cost more RUs. Let's walk through a short query example that you can paste into Data Explorer. Use point reads when possible for single-item fetches; for collection queries, ensure you have helpful indexes. After you run queries, inspect Query Stats and note the RU charge; if it's high, consider adding a composite index or including the partition key in the filter. Closing question: when you see a high RU charge for a query, which three actions will you consider first: add an index, include partition filter, or increase RUs?

Monitor RU impact by comparing RU charge before and after policy changes. A misconception is to remove too many indexes to save write RU at the expense of expensive read queries — balance is key. Final question: when you observe high RU reads on a frequent query, which indexing change would you try first?

Cosmos DB provides five well-defined consistency levels: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual. Each level is a trade-off between consistency guarantees and latency/availability. Strong consistency gives the most synchronous guarantee: reads always reflect the latest committed write, but it increases cross-region latency and reduces availability in certain failure scenarios. Bounded Staleness guarantees reads lag by no more than a specified version or time window. Session consistency is a practical default for many applications because it guarantees monotonic reads and read-your-own-writes within a session while allowing better latency across regions. Consistent Prefix guarantees that reads never see out-of-order writes, and Eventual provides the weakest guarantees but the lowest latency and highest availability. A real-world example: a shopping cart that must show a user's own latest changes benefits from Session consistency, while a global analytics feed that can tolerate slight delays might use Eventual. A common misconception is that Strong is always the safest choice; in global deployments Strong can introduce unacceptable latency. Key takeaway: choose the weakest consistency that still meets your correctness requirements to reduce latency and improve availability.

Monitoring RU trends and query RU charge helps you decide whether to scale RUs, refine indexes, or change partitioning strategies.
